title: We’re still underrating 9/11’s impact
gist: Yglesias argues 9/11's world-altering impact is still underrated precisely because it was so contingent: an eccentric plot succeeded, and a shocked public was wide open to being led in almost any direction, which Bush channeled into two wars rather than inward-facing demagoguery.

insights.claim: The idea of hijacking airplanes to destroy the World Trade Center was itself an eccentric plan, so the single event that reshaped a generation of geopolitics was highly contingent rather than inevitable.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A reminder for scenario builders: tail events that reset global policy regimes often hinge on idiosyncratic choices, not structural trends.

insights.claim: Public opinion after the attack was highly malleable, and a president who wanted to channel the shock into inward-looking demagoguery rather than foreign war could have done so.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Post-shock policy direction is leadership-determined, not predetermined — the key variable to forecast after any national trauma is who holds the agenda-setting microphone.
insights.quote: If Bush had wanted to whip people up into an inward-looking demagogic fervor instead of an external-facing one, he clearly could have accomplished that, too.
insights.locator: But it was an emotionally distressing time

insights.claim: Immediately after a mass-casualty shock, the range of possible political outcomes is extremely wide and populations are willing to be led in many directions.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Treat post-shock political regimes as high-variance; cross-asset hedges should assume wide policy dispersion rather than a single base case.
insights.quote: War on Terror 1 was crazy, and people were prepared to be led in all kinds of directions.
insights.locator: But it was an emotionally distressing time

themes.theme: Popularity of the wars, retroactively denied

insights.claim: Invading Iraq had 70 percent approval in March and April of 2003, a fact critics are often now reluctant to admit.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Historical polling shows mass support for policies later treated as elite mistakes — a caution against assuming today's unpopular consensus was always unpopular.
insights.quote: Invading Iraq had 70 percent approval in March and April of 2003.
insights.locator: Critics are often reluctant to admit it now

insights.claim: The Bush administration moved the country helter-skelter into an Afghanistan war that failed in its main objectives and an Iraq war that had nothing to do with the 9/11 attack.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The canonical case study of a shock being used to justify unrelated policy — watch for the same pattern in modern crisis-driven legislation.

insights.claim: Researchers find a pronounced increase in vacancy rates at the three most iconic office buildings in Chicago after 9/11 because tenants feared other landmark buildings would be attacked.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Terror risk attaches a measurable discount to trophy assets — relevant to underwriting landmark CRE after any high-profile attack.
insights.quote: there was a pronounced increase in vacancy rates at the three most iconic office buildings in Chicago
insights.locator: Researchers find that there was a pronounced increase

insights.claim: The panic generalized far beyond New York and Washington, with an anthrax scare at M.I.T. and an anonymous threat at the Harvard campus libraries within weeks.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Contagion of fear, not physical damage, drove the bulk of the near-term economic disruption.
insights.locator: A few weeks later, there was an anthrax scare

insights.claim: Days after the attack Bush visited an Islamic center to call Islam a religion of peace and tamp down an incipient wave of hate crimes, many of which were mistakenly directed at Sikhs.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows the same presidency simultaneously restrained domestic backlash and escalated abroad — the two responses are separable policy levers.
insights.locator: A few days after the attack, George W. Bush went to an Islamic center

insights.claim: Mass simultaneous witnessing matters: large numbers of Americans literally watched thousands of people die on live television, and the footage was replayed endlessly for days afterward.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The transmission mechanism from event to political regime change is mediated imagery, not casualty counts — a lens for assessing which future events will move policy.
